t: The Stele of the Vultures records Eannatum's victory over Umma around 2450 BCE in the dispute over the Gu'edena, one of the earliest organised battles known, won by a dense phalanx of spearmen.
Urukagina, the last ruler of the First Dynasty, made judicial, social and economic reforms that may well be the first legal code known to have existed.
The Gudea cylinders found at Girsu contain the longest known text in the Sumerian language, from a reign marked by riches, power and the building of temples.
dyk: The dynasties of Lagash are missing from the Sumerian King List; the one tablet that lists its rulers, The Rulers of Lagash, is generally read as a satirical parody of the King List, its thirty kings given improbable reigns.
ev: The First Dynasty of Lagash begins; En-hegal is believed to be its first ruler, followed by Lugalshaengur, named an ensi of Lagash on a mace head of Mesilim, king of Kish.
Eannatum defeats the army of Umma over the fertile Gu'edena, the battle shown on the Stele of the Vultures.
Sargon of Akkad lays waste the land from Lagash to the sea; his son Rimush later reconquers the rebellious city, recording 8,049 killed and 5,460 enslaved at Ur and Lagash.
Puzur-Mama declares Lagash independent after the death of Shar-Kali-Sharri; the Second Dynasty begins.
Gudea rules a rich and powerful Lagash, builds and restores temples, campaigns against Anshan and leaves the Gudea cylinders.
Ur-Nammu of Ur slays Nam-mahani, ensi of Lagash, ending the Second Dynasty; the Lagash state becomes the largest province of the Ur III empire.

f.capital: Lagash (Al-Hiba); Girsu (Telloh), the religious centre with the E-ninnu of Ningirsu
f.predecessor: Early Dynastic I settlement at Lagash among the Sumerian cities of the early third millennium BCE
f.successor: The Third Dynasty of Ur, under which the Lagash state became the empire's largest province
